notes.front: What is a computer network?
notes.back: A collection of autonomous computers interconnected by a single technology, able to exchange information.

notes.front: Define PAN (Personal Area Network).
notes.back: A network covering the range of a single person, e.g. Bluetooth linking a phone, headset, and watch.

notes.front: Define LAN (Local Area Network).
notes.back: A privately owned network operating within a single building or campus, typically up to a few km, e.g. Ethernet or Wi-Fi.

notes.front: Define MAN (Metropolitan Area Network).
notes.back: A network spanning a city, e.g. cable television networks or city-wide Wi-Fi.

notes.front: Define WAN (Wide Area Network).
notes.back: A network spanning a large geographical area, often a country or continent, connecting hosts via a subnet of routers and communication lines.

notes.front: What distinguishes a WAN from a LAN in Tanenbaum's classification?
notes.back: A WAN spans a large geographical area and consists of hosts connected by a subnet (routers + transmission lines); a LAN is confined to a building/campus.

notes.front: What is the internet (lowercase i) as defined by Tanenbaum?
notes.back: A network of networks, interconnected via routers following common protocols so they function as one large network.

notes.front: What is a subnet in the WAN context?
notes.back: The collection of routers and communication lines owned by the network operator, separate from the hosts that connect to it.

notes.front: What are the two broad categories of network transmission technology?
notes.back: Broadcast links (shared channel, all machines receive all packets) and point-to-point links (individual connections between pairs of machines).

notes.front: What is a broadcast network?
notes.back: A network with a single shared communication channel where packets sent by any machine are received by all others; addressing determines the intended recipient.

notes.front: What are the sub-types of broadcast addressing?
notes.back: Unicasting (one destination), multicasting (a subset of machines), and broadcasting (all machines).

notes.front: What is the difference between store-and-forward (packet) switching and circuit switching?
notes.back: Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path for the duration of a call; packet switching stores and forwards discrete packets independently, sharing capacity dynamically.

notes.front: What is the OSI Reference Model?
notes.back: A 7-layer conceptual model (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) for structuring network protocols, developed by ISO.

notes.front: List the 7 layers of the OSI model in order (bottom to top).
notes.back: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

notes.front: What is the role of the Physical layer (OSI Layer 1)?
notes.back: Transmitting raw bits over a communication channel.

notes.front: What is the role of the Data Link layer (OSI Layer 2)?
notes.back: Transforming a raw transmission facility into a line free of undetected transmission errors; framing, error control, flow control.

notes.front: What is the role of the Network layer (OSI Layer 3)?
notes.back: Controlling subnet operation: routing packets from source to destination, congestion control.

notes.front: What is the role of the Transport layer (OSI Layer 4)?
notes.back: Accepting data from the session layer, splitting it into smaller units if needed, and ensuring the pieces arrive correctly at the other end; end-to-end delivery.

notes.front: What is the role of the Session layer (OSI Layer 5)?
notes.back: Establishing sessions between users, including dialog control, token management, and synchronization.

notes.front: What is the role of the Presentation layer (OSI Layer 6)?
notes.back: Concerned with the syntax and semantics of transmitted data, e.g. data encoding, encryption, compression.

notes.front: What is the role of the Application layer (OSI Layer 7)?
notes.back: Contains protocols that are commonly needed by users, e.g. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol), FTP (File Transfer Protocol), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol).

notes.front: What is the TCP/IP Reference Model layers (bottom to top)?
notes.back: Link, Internet, Transport, Application.

notes.front: What is the Internet layer in the TCP/IP model responsible for?
notes.back: Delivering IP (Internet Protocol) packets to their destination; defines an official packet format and protocol called IP; handles routing.

notes.front: Name the two main Transport layer protocols in the TCP/IP model.
notes.back: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) - reliable, connection-oriented; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) - unreliable, connectionless.

notes.front: What key criticism does Tanenbaum raise about the OSI model's practical adoption?
notes.back: The OSI protocols themselves were never widely adopted in practice, largely because the timing, technology, politics, and complexity worked against them; the model outlived the protocols.

notes.front: What is meant by 'protocol layering'?
notes.back: Organizing communication functions into a stack of layers, each providing services to the layer above and using services from the layer below via defined interfaces.

notes.front: What is a 'service' vs a 'protocol' in layered network architecture?
notes.back: A service is the set of operations a layer offers to the layer above (interface); a protocol is the set of rules governing the format and meaning of messages exchanged between peer entities at the same layer.

notes.front: What is an SDU vs a PDU?
notes.back: SDU (Service Data Unit) is the data passed down to a layer to be transmitted; PDU (Protocol Data Unit) is the unit exchanged between peer layers, typically the SDU plus a protocol header.

notes.front: What is Metcalfe's Law?
notes.back: The value of a network is proportional to the square of the number of connected users (n(n-1) possible connections).

notes.front: What is bandwidth in networking?
notes.back: The amount of data (in bits per second) that can be transmitted over a channel in a given time; the data rate/capacity of a link.

notes.front: What is latency?
notes.back: The time it takes for a bit of data to travel from sender to receiver across a network.

notes.front: What does the Physical layer transmit?
notes.back: Raw bits over a physical transmission medium, without regard to their meaning.

notes.front: What is Fourier analysis used for in the context of signal transmission?
notes.back: Decomposing a periodic signal into its constituent sine wave frequency components, used to analyze how a channel's bandwidth affects signal transmission.

notes.front: What is the Nyquist theorem (noiseless channel)?
notes.back: For a noiseless channel of bandwidth H, the maximum data rate is 2H log2(V) bits/sec, where V is the number of discrete signal levels.

notes.front: What is the Shannon capacity theorem (noisy channel)?
notes.back: The maximum data rate of a channel with bandwidth H and signal-to-noise ratio S/N is C = H log2(1 + S/N) bits/sec.

notes.front: What is twisted pair cable and its main issue?
notes.back: Two insulated copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference from adjacent pairs (crosstalk); relatively low bandwidth and susceptible to noise.

notes.front: What is the difference between Category 5 (Cat 5) and Category 6 (Cat 6) twisted pair cable?
notes.back: Cat 6 has tighter twists and better shielding, supporting higher bandwidths (up to 10 Gbps) over shorter distances compared to Cat 5.

notes.front: What is coaxial cable?
notes.back: A cable with a solid copper core, insulator, braided outer conductor, and protective sheath, offering better shielding and higher bandwidth than twisted pair.

notes.front: How does fiber optic transmission work?
notes.back: Light pulses travel through a thin glass or plastic fiber via total internal reflection, encoding 1s and 0s as light presence/absence.

notes.front: What are the two types of fiber optic cable?
notes.back: Multimode fiber (multiple light paths/rays, shorter distances) and single-mode fiber (single light path, longer distances, more expensive).

notes.front: What is attenuation in signal transmission?
notes.back: The loss of signal strength as it travels over a medium, typically expressed in decibels (dB) per unit distance.

notes.front: What is the electromagnetic spectrum's role in wireless transmission?
notes.back: Different frequency bands (radio, microwave, infrared, visible light) have different propagation properties and are allocated for different wireless transmission uses.

notes.front: What is a communication satellite geostationary orbit used for?
notes.back: Placing satellites at ~35,800 km altitude above the equator so they appear stationary relative to Earth, useful for broadcast and long-haul communication, at the cost of high latency (~270ms one-way).

notes.front: What is the difference between GEO, MEO, and LEO satellites?
notes.back: GEO (Geostationary Earth Orbit, ~35,800 km, high latency), MEO (Medium Earth Orbit, e.g. GPS satellites), and LEO (Low Earth Orbit, ~750-1500 km, low latency, used by constellations like Starlink).

notes.front: What is PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network)?
notes.back: The traditional circuit-switched telephone network originally designed for voice, later adapted to carry data.

notes.front: What is a modem?
notes.back: A device that MOdulates and DEModulates a digital signal onto/from an analog carrier signal for transmission over analog lines like telephone lines.

notes.front: What is DSL (Digital Subscriber Line)?
notes.back: A technology that uses the existing twisted-pair telephone local loop to deliver high-bandwidth digital data by using frequencies above the voice band.

notes.front: What is ADSL (Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line)?
notes.back: A DSL variant offering different (asymmetric) upload and download bandwidths, typically much faster downstream than upstream.

notes.front: What is DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification)?
notes.back: The standard allowing high-speed data transmission over existing cable television (coax) infrastructure.

notes.front: What is frequency division multiplexing (FDM)?
notes.back: Dividing the available bandwidth of a channel into separate frequency bands, allowing multiple signals to be transmitted simultaneously without interference.

notes.front: What is time division multiplexing (TDM)?
notes.back: Dividing channel usage into time slots, with each user/signal transmitting during its assigned slot on the full frequency band.

notes.front: What is wavelength division multiplexing (WDM)?
notes.back: The optical fiber equivalent of FDM: multiple light wavelengths (colors) carry independent data streams simultaneously over a single fiber.

notes.front: What is code division multiple access (CDMA)?
notes.back: A multiplexing technique where each transmitter is assigned a unique code (chip sequence), allowing multiple signals to share the same frequency band simultaneously and be separated by the receiver via the codes.

notes.front: What is switching in the context of the phone system?
notes.back: The process of routing a call through intermediate switching offices to establish a path (circuit) between caller and callee.

notes.front: What is a local loop?
notes.back: The final segment of twisted-pair copper wire connecting a subscriber's premises to the telephone company's local switching office (also called 'last mile').

notes.front: What is the main goal of the Data Link layer?
notes.back: To provide a well-defined service interface to the network layer, deal with transmission errors, and regulate data flow so slow receivers aren't overwhelmed by fast senders.

notes.front: What is framing in the Data Link layer?
notes.back: Breaking the bit stream from the physical layer into discrete frames, computing a checksum for each, and verifying it at the receiver.

notes.front: Name four framing methods.
notes.back: Byte count, flag bytes with byte stuffing, flag bits with bit stuffing, and physical layer coding violations.

notes.front: What is byte stuffing?
notes.back: Inserting a special escape byte before any byte in the payload that accidentally matches a flag byte, so the receiver can distinguish data from delimiters.

notes.front: What is bit stuffing?
notes.back: After five consecutive 1 bits in the data, the sender inserts a 0 bit; the receiver removes any 0 that follows five consecutive 1s, preventing data from mimicking the flag pattern (e.g. 01111110).

notes.front: What is the purpose of error-detecting codes vs error-correcting codes?
notes.back: Error-detecting codes allow the receiver to detect (but not fix) errors, requesting retransmission; error-correcting codes (like Hamming codes) contain enough redundancy for the receiver to deduce the correct data without retransmission.

notes.front: What is a Hamming code?
notes.back: An error-correcting code that adds parity bits at specific positions so that any single-bit error can be detected and corrected by the receiver.

notes.front: What is Hamming distance?
notes.back: The number of bit positions in which two codewords differ; determines a code's error detection/correction capability.

notes.front: What is a CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)?
notes.back: An error-detecting code that treats the frame as a polynomial and computes a remainder after division by a generator polynomial, appended to the frame to detect burst errors.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a checksum in general?
notes.back: A value computed from data to detect changes/errors introduced during transmission or storage.

notes.front: What is flow control?
notes.back: A mechanism to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's buffer, e.g. via feedback-based or rate-based schemes.

notes.front: What is the Stop-and-Wait protocol?
notes.back: A simple flow control protocol where the sender transmits one frame and waits for an acknowledgment before sending the next.

notes.front: What is a Sliding Window protocol?
notes.back: A protocol allowing the sender to transmit multiple frames (up to a window size) before needing acknowledgment, improving throughput over stop-and-wait.

notes.front: What is Go-Back-N ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)?
notes.back: A sliding window protocol where, upon a lost/errored frame, the receiver discards it and all subsequent frames, and the sender retransmits from that frame onward.

notes.front: What is Selective Repeat ARQ?
notes.back: A sliding window protocol where only the specific erroneous or lost frame is retransmitted, and correctly received out-of-order frames are buffered at the receiver.

notes.front: What is piggybacking in sliding window protocols?
notes.back: Attaching an acknowledgment for received data onto an outgoing data frame in the reverse direction, rather than sending a separate ACK frame.

notes.front: What determines the optimal sender window size in a sliding window protocol?
notes.back: It should be large enough to keep the pipe full given the bandwidth-delay product, i.e., at least (bandwidth x round-trip time)/frame size.

notes.front: What is the bandwidth-delay product?
notes.back: The product of a link's bandwidth and its round-trip propagation delay; represents the amount of data 'in flight' needed to fully utilize the link.

notes.front: What is HDLC (High-level Data Link Control)?
notes.back: A bit-oriented Data Link layer protocol using flag bytes and bit stuffing for framing, supporting flow and error control.

notes.front: What is PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol)?
notes.back: A widely used Data Link layer protocol for establishing direct point-to-point connections, e.g. over serial links or as a basis for DSL/PPPoE.

notes.front: What is the MAC (Medium Access Control) sublayer responsible for?
notes.back: Determining who gets to use a shared broadcast channel next, in multiple access networks.

notes.front: What is the difference between static and dynamic channel allocation?
notes.back: Static allocation divides the channel into fixed portions per user (e.g. FDM); dynamic allocation assigns channel access on demand based on traffic.

notes.front: What is ALOHA (pure ALOHA)?
notes.back: A random access protocol where stations transmit whenever they have data, and retransmit after a random backoff if a collision (detected via lack of ack) occurs.

notes.front: What is the maximum channel utilization of pure ALOHA?
What is Slotted ALOHA and how does it improve on pure ALOHA?
notes.back: Time is divided into discrete slots, and stations may only start transmission at slot boundaries; this doubles maximum utilization to about 36.8% (1/e).

notes.front: What does CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access) mean?
notes.back: Stations first listen to (sense) the channel before transmitting, and only transmit if the channel is idle, reducing collisions compared to ALOHA.

notes.front: What is 1-persistent CSMA?
notes.back: A station senses the channel; if idle, it transmits immediately with probability 1. If busy, it waits until idle then transmits immediately.

notes.front: What is non-persistent CSMA?
notes.back: If the channel is busy, the station waits a random amount of time before sensing again, reducing collision probability compared to 1-persistent.

notes.front: What is p-persistent CSMA?
notes.back: Used in slotted channels: if idle, the station transmits with probability p, or defers to the next slot with probability 1-p.

notes.front: What is CSMA/CD (Collision Detection)?
notes.back: A CSMA variant, used in classic Ethernet, where stations monitor the channel while transmitting and abort immediately upon detecting a collision, saving time.

notes.front: Why is CSMA/CD not used in modern switched Ethernet?
notes.back: Because full-duplex switched links have no shared collision domain — each link has a dedicated sender and receiver, so collisions cannot occur.

notes.front: What is CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance)?
notes.back: A MAC scheme (used in Wi-Fi/802.11) that avoids collisions rather than detecting them, using techniques like waiting for the channel to be idle plus a random backoff, and optionally RTS/CTS.

notes.front: What is the hidden terminal problem?
notes.back: In wireless networks, two stations that cannot hear each other might both sense the channel idle and transmit simultaneously to a common receiver, causing a collision the sender is unaware of.

notes.front: What is RTS/CTS (Request to Send / Clear to Send)?
notes.back: A handshake mechanism in wireless MAC protocols where a sender requests permission to transmit (RTS) and the receiver grants it (CTS), reserving the channel and helping mitigate the hidden terminal problem.

notes.front: What is Ethernet's classic frame format's minimum frame size and why?
notes.back: 64 bytes; it ensures that a transmitting station is still sending when a collision signal could return, so CSMA/CD collision detection works correctly given cable propagation delay.

notes.front: What is the MAC address?
notes.back: A globally unique 48-bit hardware address assigned to a network interface, used for addressing frames on the local network segment.

notes.front: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
notes.back: A hub is a physical-layer device that repeats signals to all ports (single collision domain); a switch is a Data Link layer device that forwards frames only to the relevant port based on MAC address, creating separate collision domains.

notes.front: What is VLAN (Virtual LAN)?
notes.back: A technique for logically partitioning a physical LAN into multiple isolated broadcast domains, regardless of physical switch port location.

notes.front: What is the Spanning Tree Protocol used for?
notes.back: Preventing loops in networks with redundant switch links by constructing a loop-free logical topology (spanning tree) while retaining redundancy for failover.

notes.front: What is the difference between a bridge and a switch?
notes.back: Functionally similar (both forward frames based on MAC address at the Data Link layer); 'switch' commonly refers to multiport bridges used in modern LANs.

notes.front: What are the two main services the Network layer can offer?
notes.back: Connectionless service (datagram, e.g. IP) and connection-oriented service (virtual circuit).

notes.front: What is a virtual circuit?
notes.back: A pre-established logical path through the subnet for a connection, along which all packets of that connection travel, avoiding per-packet routing decisions.

notes.front: What is a datagram subnet?
notes.back: A connectionless subnet where each packet is routed independently based on its destination address, with no pre-established path.

notes.front: What is a routing algorithm's main job?
notes.back: Deciding which output line an incoming packet should be transmitted on, i.e., determining the path packets take through the subnet.

notes.front: What is the difference between adaptive and non-adaptive routing?
notes.back: Adaptive routing changes decisions based on current network state/traffic; non-adaptive (static) routing uses fixed, pre-computed routes.

notes.front: What is the Shortest Path Routing algorithm (Dijkstra)?
notes.back: An algorithm that computes the shortest path from a source to all other nodes in a graph with non-negative edge weights, used as a basis for many routing protocols.

notes.front: What is Distance Vector Routing?
notes.back: Each router maintains a table of best known distance to each destination and next hop, periodically exchanging this table with neighbors (e.g. RIP - Routing Information Protocol).

notes.front: What is the 'count-to-infinity' problem in Distance Vector Routing?
notes.back: A failure scenario where routers slowly increment their distance estimates to an unreachable destination in a loop, converging very slowly to infinity.

notes.front: What is Link State Routing?
notes.back: Each router discovers its neighbors, measures link costs, floods this link-state information to all routers, and each independently computes shortest paths (e.g. via Dijkstra's algorithm); used in OSPF.

notes.front: What is OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)?
notes.back: A link-state interior gateway routing protocol widely used within autonomous systems, using Dijkstra's algorithm to compute shortest paths.

notes.front: What is BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)?
notes.back: The exterior gateway (path-vector) routing protocol used to exchange routing information between autonomous systems on the internet.

notes.front: What is an Autonomous System (AS)?
notes.back: A network or group of networks under a single administrative control, using a common interior routing policy.

notes.front: What is hierarchical routing?
notes.back: Organizing routers into regions/clusters to reduce routing table size and update overhead, at the cost of potentially suboptimal paths.

notes.front: What is congestion in a network?
notes.back: A condition where too many packets are present in (a part of) the subnet, degrading performance as delay and packet loss increase.

notes.front: What is the difference between congestion control and flow control?
notes.back: Congestion control manages overall traffic load on the network/subnet; flow control manages the rate between a specific sender and receiver so the receiver isn't overwhelmed.

notes.front: What is a leaky bucket algorithm?
notes.back: A traffic shaping mechanism where packets are queued and released onto the network at a constant, fixed output rate, regardless of burstiness of input.

notes.front: What is a token bucket algorithm?
notes.back: A traffic shaping mechanism where tokens accumulate at a fixed rate in a bucket; a packet can be sent only if a token is available, allowing some burstiness unlike the leaky bucket.

notes.front: What is RED (Random Early Detection/Discard)?
notes.back: A congestion avoidance mechanism where routers proactively drop (or mark) packets probabilistically as queue length grows, signaling senders to slow down before the queue fully overflows.

notes.front: What is IP (Internet Protocol)?
notes.back: The Network layer protocol of the internet, providing connectionless, best-effort delivery of packets (datagrams) identified by IP addresses.

notes.front: What is an IPv4 address?
notes.back: A 32-bit address, typically written in dotted-decimal notation, identifying a host's interface on the internet.

notes.front: What is CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)?
notes.back: An addressing scheme that replaced the old class-based IP addressing, using a network prefix length (e.g. /24) to allow flexible allocation of address blocks and aggregate routing.

notes.front: What is NAT (Network Address Translation)?
notes.back: A technique allowing multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address by rewriting address/port information in packets as they cross the network boundary.

notes.front: What is subnetting?
notes.back: Dividing a single IP network into smaller sub-networks (subnets) by borrowing bits from the host portion of the address for additional network identification.

notes.front: Why was IPv6 developed?
notes.back: Primarily to solve IPv4 address exhaustion by expanding the address space to 128 bits, while also simplifying the header and improving support for real-time traffic and security.

notes.front: What is an IPv6 address size?
notes.back: 128 bits, typically written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.

notes.front: What is ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol)?
notes.back: A protocol used by hosts and routers to report errors and exchange control/diagnostic information, e.g. ping (echo request/reply) and destination unreachable messages.

notes.front: What is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)?
notes.back: A protocol used to map an IP address to its corresponding MAC address on a local network.

notes.front: What is DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)?
notes.back: A protocol that automatically assigns IP addresses and other configuration parameters (subnet mask, gateway, DNS) to hosts on a network.

notes.front: What is MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching)?
notes.back: A technique that forwards packets based on short fixed-length labels rather than full network address lookups, enabling faster forwarding and traffic engineering.

notes.front: What is anycast addressing?
notes.back: An addressing scheme where a single address is assigned to multiple devices, and traffic is routed to the topologically nearest instance.

notes.front: What is the primary role of the Transport layer?
notes.back: Providing reliable, efficient, end-to-end data transport between application processes, hiding the details of the underlying network from the layers above.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Network layer and Transport layer in terms of control?
notes.back: The Network layer is typically run by carriers/ISPs (outside end-user control); the Transport layer runs on the end hosts, giving applications control over reliability and delivery guarantees.

notes.front: What is a socket?
notes.back: An endpoint for network communication identified by an IP address and port number, used by applications to send/receive data via the Transport layer.

notes.front: What is TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?
notes.back: A connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream Transport layer protocol providing in-order delivery, error checking, flow control, and congestion control.

notes.front: What is UDP (User Datagram Protocol)?
notes.back: A connectionless, unreliable Transport layer protocol providing minimal overhead with no guarantees of delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection.

notes.front: What is the TCP three-way handshake?
notes.back: The connection establishment process: client sends SYN, server responds SYN-ACK, client responds ACK, after which the connection is established.

notes.front: What is TCP connection teardown ('four-way handshake')?
notes.back: Each side independently sends a FIN when done sending, and the other acknowledges it, since TCP connections are full-duplex and each direction closes separately.

notes.front: What is TCP's sliding window used for?
notes.back: Flow control and reliable delivery: it defines how much unacknowledged data the sender may have in flight, advertised by the receiver based on its available buffer space.

notes.front: What is the TCP 'silly window syndrome' and how is it addressed?
notes.back: A performance problem where small amounts of data are sent/acknowledged repeatedly in tiny segments; addressed via Nagle's algorithm (sender) and delayed ACK / avoiding tiny window advertisements (receiver).

notes.front: What is Nagle's algorithm?
notes.back: A TCP sender optimization that delays sending small segments, buffering data until an ACK is received or a full segment can be sent, reducing overhead from many tiny packets.

notes.front: What is TCP congestion control's 'slow start' phase?
notes.back: The sender starts with a small congestion window and exponentially increases it for each successful RTT (Round-Trip Time) until reaching a threshold or detecting loss.

notes.front: What happens after slow start reaches the ssthresh (slow start threshold)?
notes.back: TCP switches to congestion avoidance, increasing the congestion window linearly (additive increase) rather than exponentially.

notes.front: What is AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease)?
notes.back: A TCP congestion control strategy: increase the congestion window linearly on success, but cut it drastically (e.g. halve it) upon detecting congestion/loss.

notes.front: What is a duplicate ACK in TCP, and what does receiving three trigger?
notes.back: An ACK repeating the same acknowledgment number, indicating a later segment arrived out of order; three duplicate ACKs typically trigger TCP's 'fast retransmit' of the missing segment.

notes.front: What is TCP fast recovery?
notes.back: After fast retransmit, instead of returning to slow start, TCP halves the congestion window and resumes with linear increase, avoiding a full restart.

notes.front: What is RTO (Retransmission TimeOut) in TCP?
notes.back: The time TCP waits for an ACK before assuming a segment was lost and retransmitting it; dynamically computed from measured RTT and its variance.

notes.front: What is the TCP header's checksum used for?
notes.back: Detecting errors in the TCP segment (header + data) during transmission, computed over a pseudo-header plus the segment.

notes.front: What is a TCP port number, and what range are 'well-known ports'?
notes.back: A 16-bit number identifying a specific process/service on a host; well-known ports are 0-1023, reserved for standard services (e.g. 80 for HTTP).

notes.front: What is QUIC?
notes.back: A modern transport protocol built on UDP, providing reliability, multiplexed streams, and built-in encryption (TLS), designed to reduce connection setup latency compared to TCP+TLS.

notes.front: What is head-of-line blocking in the context of TCP?
notes.back: A situation where a single lost segment delays the delivery of all subsequent, already-received data to the application, since TCP guarantees in-order delivery.

notes.front: What is the purpose of sequence numbers in TCP?
notes.back: To allow the receiver to reorder out-of-order segments, detect duplicates, and acknowledge exactly how much data has been received in order.

notes.front: What is DNS (Domain Name System)?
notes.back: A hierarchical, distributed naming system that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses.

notes.front: What is the structure of the DNS hierarchy?
notes.back: A tree rooted at the root zone, then top-level domains (TLDs, e.g. .com, .org), then second-level domains, and further subdomains.

notes.front: What is a DNS resolver?
notes.back: A client-side component (or recursive server) that queries the DNS hierarchy on behalf of an application to resolve a domain name to an IP address.

notes.front: What is the difference between a recursive and an iterative DNS query?
notes.back: In a recursive query, the queried server takes full responsibility for obtaining the final answer (querying others itself); in an iterative query, it returns the best answer it has (often a referral) and lets the client continue querying.

notes.front: What is a DNS record type 'A'?
notes.back: A record mapping a hostname to an IPv4 address.

notes.front: What is a DNS record type 'AAAA'?
notes.back: A record mapping a hostname to an IPv6 address.

notes.front: What is a DNS MX record?
notes.back: A record specifying the mail exchange server(s) responsible for receiving email for a domain.

notes.front: What is HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)?
notes.back: An application-layer protocol for transferring hypertext (web) documents, based on a request-response model between clients and servers.

notes.front: What is the difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2?
notes.back: HTTP/2 introduces binary framing, multiplexing multiple requests/responses over a single TCP connection, and header compression, addressing HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking and connection overhead.

notes.front: What is a persistent HTTP connection?
notes.back: A TCP connection kept open across multiple HTTP requests/responses, avoiding the overhead of establishing a new connection for each request.

notes.front: What is a cookie in HTTP?
notes.back: A small piece of state data sent by a server and stored by the client, returned on subsequent requests to maintain session state, since HTTP itself is stateless.

notes.front: What is SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)?
notes.back: An application-layer protocol used to send/relay email messages between mail servers.

notes.front: What is the difference between SMTP and POP3/IMAP?
notes.back: SMTP is used to send/relay mail between servers; POP3 (Post Office Protocol) and IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) are used by a client to retrieve/manage mail from a mailbox server.

notes.front: What is FTP (File Transfer Protocol)?
notes.back: An application-layer protocol for transferring files between a client and server, traditionally using separate control and data connections.

notes.front: What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
notes.back: A geographically distributed network of servers that cache and deliver content from locations closer to end users, reducing latency and load on origin servers.

notes.front: What is peer-to-peer (P2P) networking?
notes.back: A distributed application architecture where participants (peers) act as both clients and servers, sharing resources directly with each other rather than through a central server.

notes.front: What is a BitTorrent 'tracker'?
notes.back: A server that helps peers in a torrent swarm discover each other, without itself hosting the actual file content.

notes.front: What is streaming media, and how does it differ from downloading?
notes.back: Streaming media is played back progressively as it is received, without requiring the entire file to be downloaded first.

notes.front: What is TLS (Transport Layer Security)?
notes.back: A cryptographic protocol providing confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for application-layer data, commonly used to secure HTTP (as HTTPS) atop TCP.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a URL (Uniform Resource Locator)?
notes.back: To specify the location of a resource on the internet, including scheme (protocol), host, port, path, and optional query parameters.
